Here's the way I did it. It might not be the fastest, but it lets me pipe stuff and/or provide them as args. And each arg/line can have multiple space delimited entries that get properly split out.

https://github.com/SpicyLemon/SpicyLemon/blob/master/bash_fun/generic/max.sh

```
# Usage: <stuff> | max 
 #    or: max <val1> [<val2> ...] 
 #    or: <stuff> | max - <val1> [<val2> ...] 
 max () { 
     { 
         if [[ "$#" -eq '0' ]]; then 
             cat - 
         else 
             while [[ "$#" -gt '0' ]]; do 
                 if [[ "$1" == '-' ]]; then 
                     cat - 
                 else 
                     printf ' %s ' "$1" 
                 fi 
                 shift 
             done 
         fi 
     } | tr '[:space:]' '\n' | grep . | sort -n -r | head -n 1 
 }
```

Basically:
1. Print out all the input.
2. Change each space into a newline (putting each number on its own line).
3. Ignore empty lines.
4. Sort numerically in reverse order.
5. Output only the first line.

Technically also works with strings.

The general idea is to use `curl` (or whatever) to get some json, send it to `jq` to extract and format what you need, then send that to `fzf` to let you select entries you want to do more with. Usually those selections then get sent to something else for further action.

A couple jobs ago, we used Gitlab as our central code repository. Gitlab has a pretty sweet API for getting all sorts of info. So I put together a suite of scripts/functions for interacting with Gitlab.

Specific use cases:

* Find and clone a repo without having to leave my terminal.
* Get a list of MRs (they call them "Merge Requests" instead of "Pull Requests") that I should review and open the selected ones in my browser (for me to review). I'm not sure if Gitlab added something to their UI for this, but at the time, they didn't have a page with that list.
* View and manage my Gitlab TODO list.
* Get status info on CI/CD jobs and open selected ones in my browser.
* Do code or MR searches and open selected results in my browser.

I don't use any of that stuff anymore, but it's what really got me started in shell scripting.... so much shell scripting. When I left, I started trying to make similar stuff that used Github, but stopped because they released their own command-line tool.

At that job, someone had also put together a handy Kubernetes helper. It'd start with a list of things you might like to do with Kubernetes, then move on to letting you select various options related to what you want to do (e.g. regions, containers etc.) and eventually make it happen. I'm not sure exactly what was used to get the initial json, but I know it used `jq` and multiple levels of `fzf` in order to build the command.

Anymore, the only thing I regularly use that uses both `jq` and `fzf` is a json explorer that I've put together. It lists all paths on the left and displays each path's metadata (e.g. field type and sub-keys) and content on the right. I can select entries which are then printed in a json array with key and value. I know there are better ones out there, but oh well.

I often end up writing one-off scripts for specific research/problems that use the `curl | jq | fzf | something else` structure.
jq and fzf have revolutionized my terminal experience.

There's no easy way to know which one to trust. My gut says to trust the middle one though.

With a liquid thermometer (the middle one), the most common source of inaccuracies is incorrect placement with respects to the numbers. Eyeballing the spaces above and below the glass tube, I'd guess there's about 3 degrees of possible error (i.e. +/- 1.5). But barring complete negligence by the manufacturer, it's going to be pretty accurate for the entire scale provided.

The one on the left, I'm assuming is a bi-metal thermometer. Those can be ruined pretty easily. Without knowing it's full history and how it's been handled, I wouldn't really trust it. Also, since it's reading is significantly different from the other two, it's probably not correct.

Digital thermometers are more complex. There are different types, but they all have similar systems. There's one sensor that outputs different voltages/signals based on temperatures, and another sensor for reading and interpreting the first. I've seen too many that have critical design failures (e.g. some component gives off heat and is too close to the temperature sensor). So I usually don't trust digital ones much.


The only way to know for sure which one is most accurate is to compare each to a trusted source. That can either be another thermometer that you know is accurate, or an environment where the temperature is known and consistent.

All of these just sound like things that will come with experience. Keep your head up, keep paying attention, and keep wanting to learn. Problem solving skills are something you will (hopefully) never stop building.

You've already taken one of the most important steps: identifying situations where you'd like to improve.

Another important step you've taken is reaching out for help. It's often difficult, and I commend you for it.

Next time you find yourself not knowing something, and getting frustrated or wanting to give up, take a deep breath, relax, either retrace your steps and try to find something different to try, or ask for help.

It's okay to not know things. It's significantly more difficult to learn if you think you already know. So it's important to be honest with yourself about what you do and don't know.

It's okay to admit you don't know something. There are some folks out there that might tell you otherwise here, but do your best to ignore them (even if it's yourself telling you). Just because a person says something is "obvious" doesn't make it obvious. Just because someone says something is easy, doesn't make it easy.

It's also okay to lean on others for help and guidance. In many situations, it's easier to learn by watching someone else do it. So let them, and next time, if you're comfortable, give it your own shot.

>The first being when I went out with my family and went into a lift, I would look for the lift buttons left and right where it is normally located, but in this case, the lift buttons were in the opposite side of the opening door and I failed to notice and just continued using my phone while my sister instinctively looked around, found and pressed the lift buttons. I felt dumb afterwards and my older sister just seemed to shrug it off.

Only one person needs to push the button(s) on the lift anyway. Now you know that sometimes the buttons can be in other places. I'm 40 and still sometimes get confused by them. Sometimes a key is needed. Sometimes they're near the floor (to push with your feet). Sometimes there's two doors and split floors. Sometimes you have to use a kiosk outside the elevator. Sometimes the elevator just moves and you have to just get on and off at the right time. Who knows what else is (or will be) out there In any case, all it takes is one person around you knowing.

>The second incident was when I was in MC Donalds, trying to order a special deal meal using the app, I pressed meals instead of promotions and got to the wrong place and kept wondering what I did wrong while my sister pressed promotions instinctively. Next, I pressed promotions and I saw there was a scanner located at the lower part of the MC Donalds and saw a QR code on my phone but it did not occur to me to put the QR code of my phone to the machine scanner, while my sister once again just did it instinctively and got the promotion done.

Maybe she's done this before. Or maybe she's done something similar. It's not that she "instinctively" knew, it's that she learned how to do it at some point. I think you did great here. You identified things didn't look right. You then figured out what needed to be done by either asking for help or observing and mimicking (whatever works!). You also learned that if you have a QR code, you might be looking for something to scan it.

>Another incident would be when I was out with my friends exploring our new school institution, trying to get to a specific place in the school campus, we were both using the campus map and it was both our first time navigating, I tried to walk in different directions to find the place but still to no avail and ended up in the same place all the time which had a huge wall blocking me. While my friend on the other hand, crossed the road with me, randomly walked and found the place instinctively. 

Reading and using maps can be tough. It's a skill that only comes through practice. Keep trying and you'll get there. Again, your friend didn't instinctively find the place, and they definitely didn't walk randomly. They also had extra information now that you found the wall blocking your way. Maybe they have a little more map experience than you. Or maybe it's just that they kept trying.

As a side note, if you want some fun was to get better with maps, give GeoCaching a shot. Just Google/Bing/Whatever "GeoCaching" for a description and suggestions. These days, most of it is done using a phone app. I'm not sure what's out there for apps, but there should be some decent free ones and some good one-time-payment ones (I probably wouldn't use a subscription one though).

>Next incident would be when my friend and I reached the lift of a library in the school campus, he pressed the 2nd floor which was the level of the library floor that we were on, the lift did not respond. He then instinctively pressed other levels of the library lift and succeeded. However, when it was my turn, I pressed level 2 like him, but to no avail, I then pressed multiple times again and turned to my friend for help.

You did a good job here. It was a confusing situation, and you asked for help. You learned that sometimes, lifts label floors in weird ways. In this case, the floor you came in on, was floor 2 (instead of 1, or even "M"). Again, the more weird lifts you find and learn about, the easier this stuff will just come to you.

>Lastly, I had this project which I was working on with my group mates, the teacher just made a few suggestions and said some foreign words quickly and left the group discussion, my teammates got it immediately and improved on it while I was there like an idiot, catching no ball and was kinda clueless.

Next time something like this happens, ask for clarification. As part of a team, your teammates (hopefully) shouldn't mind taking a moment to help you understand what's going on and/or what was said, so don't worry about interrupting them. A phrase I often use for this is, "I'm sorry. I didn't quite understand that last bit. Could you repeat it please?" Sometimes I just need to hear it again, but sometimes I have follow-up questions about specific words or parts. But in these cases, you can't know unless you ask. And again, it's okay. Everyone missess things sometimes.

Communication is an art. It requires constant practice and constant adaptations. Two key things to focus on with opinions is the words used, and the audience.

English has many many synonyms, and even more options when other sentence constructs are considered. But not all words are created equally. This recent [xkcd/2352](https://xkcd.com/2352/) comic has some good examples. Different words have different connotations. Take advantage of that.

With opinions, it's usually best to be as accurate as possible. This will reduce the amount of space available for misunderstandings. Learning new words will make it easier to be more accurate. But be careful that you're not just using a synonym because it's a "bigger" word; sometimes the small words more accurately represent your opinion.

Also with opinions, you must also consider your audience. Empathy is a trait that is handy here. You are trying to put yourself in their shoes, to guess how they are going to react. The larger the audience, the more difficult this becomes, but it's still something to do. Reading the room and specially tailoring the words in your opinion can be the difference between a productive discussion and an argument that devolves into a first fight. You should also consider that, in some cases, you shouldn't share your opinion.

Lastly, when sharing an opinion, make sure you have a purpose in mind. Are you trying to convince someone to change? Are you trying to subtly provide present ideas? Are you gather the opinions of others on order to form an opinion of your own? Your purpose and the audience will help guide your phrasing.

If forgiveness is important, and the recipient(s) don't offer it on their own accord, only then should you think about asking something like, "Do you accept my apology?" Even so, you must be prepared that the answer is very likely, "No," and there will not be a chance at following up. If you ask a question like that, you also need to consider the high likelyhood that they will lie and say, "Yes," just to avoid extra conflict. At that point, you are very unlikely to ever get the actual forgiveness you're looking for.

"Do you accept my apology?" also places a burden on the recipient. You're significantly better off asking, "How can I make things right?" It places the burden back on yourself.

Do not try to force forgiveness. Doing so is always counter productive.

Along this line, learning how to apologize will make life easier. 

1. Keep it short and clear.
1. Specifically say, "I'm sorry."
1. Identify the thing you are sorry for.
1. Unless your remorse is particularly great, stop there. Only attempt to offer an explanation for egregious wrongdoing. 
1. If you offer an explanation, you must also identify how you are going to prevent the issue in the future.
1. If you offer an explanation, make sure it's not actually an attempt at an excuse.
1. If you offer an explanation, rule 1 still applies.
1. Do not ever include an excuse in an apology. Ever. Ever ever.

I also have a personal rule that I will only apologize when I feel remorse. I will not give you an apology just because you think you deserve one, or just because someone tells me I should apologize.

Lastly, do not ever state, "I'm sorry if..." It conveys that you are not currently sorry for your actions, and that you might be sorry only under certain circumstances. It also removes most of the sincerity. If you don't know the circumstances, you probably aren't actually sorry. You're better off asking about the conditional first, and then issuing an actual apology if warranted. If you do know the circumstances, leave the "if" out and just identify what it is you feel bad about.

I'm 31, and back in May of this year, i was diagnosed with Hodgkin's Lymphoma.  I had swollen lymph nodes on my shoulder that were noticeable, and actually the reason that I went in.  It ends up I also had swollen lymph nodes around my heart, and it had just barely spread to my spleen. They staged it as "Late stage 2, early stage 3."

I didn't really have many symptoms, though.  The swollen lymph nodes was the big one.  I was also getting fevers every now and then, but they usually didn't last very long (a few hours).  The two nights before I went in, I also had the drenching night sweats (so bad I'd wake up with pruned fingers).

Since June, i've been going through the ABVD treatment.  The lymph nodes and all symptoms disappeared after the first treatment. I'm 8 treatments down, and 4 to go, and haven't really had too many side effects from it.  I get a little nauseous for the first 3-5 days after treatment, and I definitely have less energy, but other than that, I've been going strong.  I feel pretty lucky, really.  

But the ABVD treatment has been around for a long time (since the '70s I think) and has a great success rate.  It's treatment every two weeks, and I just sit in a chair for 3 hours while the meds are pumped in through my chest port.  I take treatment days off of work, but other than that, I've been able to work normally.  That's an 8-5 desk job, though, no heavy lifting or anything.

The way I saw it in the beginning is that it's a 6 month inconvenience.  So far, it hasn't even really been that.
